provenance.verification: See docs/functions-original-20261030.md for checks actually performed.

marking_policy: Maths4U indicative marking guidance, not an official examination-board mark scheme. Award stated criteria once each, up to the part maximum. Accept valid equivalent methods. lessons.title: Inverse functions, domain and range
lessons.objective: Reverse a one-to-one function and state where the inverse is defined.
lessons.notes_html:
Before you start: rearrange a linear equation and distinguish an input from an output. A domain is the set of permitted inputs; a range is the set of outputs actually attained.

An inverse reverses the input-output mapping. It is a function only when each attained output comes from one input: the original function must be one-to-one on its stated domain. In \(f^{-1}(x)\), the exponent \(-1\) denotes an inverse, not a reciprocal.

Write \(y=f(x)\), solve for \(x\), then exchange the variable names. The domain of \(f^{-1}\) is the range of \(f\), and the range of \(f^{-1}\) is the domain of \(f\). Check both the algebra and these sets.

For a fractional function, retain the excluded denominator value. Rewriting \((ax+b)/(x-c)\) as a constant plus a nonzero multiple of \(1/(x-c)\) can reveal a missing range value.

Recall later

Find the inverse of \(7-2x\) for \(0\le x\le3\). Check: \((7-x)/2\), with inverse domain \([1,7]\).

examples.question_html: Find the inverse of \(f(x)=4x-7\), for real \(x\).
examples.solution_html: From \(y=4x-7\), \(x=(y+7)/4\). Therefore \(f^{-1}(x)=(x+7)/4\), with domain and range both \(\mathbb R\). Substitution gives \(f(f^{-1}(x))=x\).
\(y(x-2)=x+1\), so \(x(y-1)=2y+1\). Thus \(f^{-1}(x)=(2x+1)/(x-1)\), with domain \(x\ne1\). The original form \(1+3/(x-2)\) shows why its range excludes 1.

examples.question_html: Find the range and inverse domain of \(f(x)=9-2x\), \(1\le x\le5\).
examples.solution_html: The function decreases. Its endpoint outputs are 7 and −1, so its range is \([-1,7]\). The inverse is \((9-x)/2\), defined for \(-1\le x\le7\), with range \([1,5]\).

common_mistakes: Giving the old domain to the inverse without finding the original range.
Cancelling or rearranging away an excluded denominator value.

lessons.title: Composite functions and their domains
lessons.objective: Apply functions in the correct order and check the intermediate value.
lessons.notes_html:
Before you start: substitute an expression into a formula and solve a linear inequality.

We use \(fg(x)=f(g(x))\): apply \(g\) first, then \(f\). It is not multiplication. Replace every input in the outer formula by the entire inner expression, using brackets.

The domain of \(fg\) consists of inputs in the domain of \(g\) whose outputs lie in the domain of \(f\). For example, a square-root outer function requires the complete inner expression to be nonnegative.

In general \(fg\ne gf\). When solving \(fg(x)=gf(x)\), use the common domain. Inverse compositions give the identity only on the appropriate original or inverse domain.

Recall later

If \(f(x)=x+4\) and \(g(x)=2x\), compare \(fg(x)=2x+4\) and \(gf(x)=2x+8\).

examples.solution_html: \(fg(x)=3(x^2-1)+2=3x^2-1\). In the other order, \(gf(x)=(3x+2)^2-1=9x^2+12x+3\). Both domains are \(\mathbb R\).
\(fg(x)=\sqrt{x-4}\) requires \(x\ge4\). But \(gf(x)=\sqrt{x}-4\) only requires \(x\ge0\). The same two functions can produce different domains in different orders.
The inverse is \(f^{-1}(x)=(x-3)/2\). Hence \(f(f^{-1}(x))=2[(x-3)/2]+3=x\). All real inputs are permitted here.

common_mistakes: Treating fg as a product or reversing the agreed order.
Checking only the final simplified formula and overlooking the intermediate domain.

lessons.title: Restricting a quadratic to obtain an inverse
lessons.objective: Choose a one-to-one branch and use the correct square-root sign.
lessons.notes_html:
Before you start: complete the square and interpret a vertex.

A full quadratic parabola is not one-to-one: inputs on opposite sides of its vertex can have the same output. Restricting the domain to one side of the vertex gives a one-to-one function.

For \(f(x)=(x-h)^2+k\) on \(x\ge h\), solving \(y=f(x)\) gives \(x=h+\sqrt{y-k}\). On \(x\le h\), use \(x=h-\sqrt{y-k}\). A function inverse uses one branch, not both signs.

The inverse domain is \(x\ge k\) for either full half-parabola. Its range remembers the chosen original branch. Additional endpoint restrictions must also be transferred.

Recall later

For \(f(x)=(x-5)^2+1\), \(x\le5\), the inverse is \(5-\sqrt{x-1}\), defined for \(x\ge1\).

examples.solution_html: Since the original input satisfies \(x+1\ge0\), take the positive root: \(x=\sqrt y-1\). Thus \(f^{-1}(x)=\sqrt{x}-1\), with domain \(x\ge0\) and range \(y\ge-1\).
Here \(x-4\le0\), so \(x=4-\sqrt{y-2}\). The inverse is \(4-\sqrt{x-2}\), with domain \(x\ge2\) and range \(y\le4\).

examples.question_html: Why does \(f(x)=x^2\) on \(\mathbb R\) have no function inverse?
examples.solution_html: Both −2 and 2 map to 4. Reversing this would give two outputs for one input. On the restricted domain \(x\ge0\), the inverse is \(\sqrt{x}\); on \(x\le0\), it is \(-\sqrt{x}\).

common_mistakes: Keeping both square-root signs in a function inverse.
Choosing the positive branch despite an original input below the vertex.
Giving the inverse range as all real numbers after restricting the original domain.

lessons.title: A function and its inverse on a graph
lessons.objective: Reflect coordinates and interpret common points without assuming a false general rule.
lessons.notes_html:
Before you start: plot coordinates and solve simultaneous equations.

If \((a,b)\) lies on \(y=f(x)\), then \((b,a)\) lies on \(y=f^{-1}(x)\). The graphs are reflections in \(y=x\). Swap vertices and endpoints as well as ordinary points; transfer domain and range restrictions.

A fixed point solves \(f(x)=x\) and lies on both graphs. For a strictly increasing real function, every common point must be on \(y=x\): if \(f(x)=y\) and \(f(y)=x\), then \(x

Do not use that conclusion for every invertible function. A decreasing function can have common points off \(y=x\); for example \(f(x)=6-x\) is its own inverse, so the two entire graphs coincide.

Recall later

Reflect \((-2,5)\) in \(y=x\): the image is \((5,-2)\). The signs stay attached to their coordinates.

examples.question_html: The graph of \(f(x)=2x+2\) contains \((1,4)\) and \((3,8)\). Locate the reflected points.
examples.solution_html: The inverse graph contains \((4,1)\) and \((8,3)\). Its equation is \(y=(x-2)/2\). The common fixed point solves \(2x+2=x\), giving \((-2,-2)\).
Its vertex \((2,1)\) becomes \((1,2)\); its point \((3,2)\) becomes \((2,3)\). The inverse is \(y=2+\sqrt{x-1}\), \(x\ge1\), with \(y\ge2\).

examples.question_html: Find the inverse of \(f(x)=6-x\) and describe the two graphs.
examples.solution_html: Rearranging \(y=6-x\) gives \(x=6-y\), so \(f^{-1}(x)=6-x\). The graphs coincide. For example \((1,5)\) is common even though it is not on \(y=x\).

common_mistakes: Reflecting in an axis rather than y=x.
Swapping the coordinates but dropping a branch restriction.
Assuming every intersection with an inverse is a fixed point, even for decreasing functions.

lessons.title: Transformations, stretches and coordinate rules
lessons.objective: Track changes inside and outside a function, including domains and ranges.
lessons.notes_html:
Before you start: read a graph's domain and range and rearrange a linear equation.

Changes outside \(f\) act on outputs: \(af(x)+b\) maps \(y\) to \(ay+b\). Changes inside act on inputs: for \(f(cx+d)\), a point with old input \(u\) has new input \((u-d)/c\), provided \(c\ne0\).

\[y=af(cx+d)+b:\qquad (u,v)\longmapsto\left(\frac{u-d}{c},av+b\right).\]

Thus \(f(x-h)\) moves a graph right by \(h\); \(f(cx)\) gives a horizontal scale factor \(1/|c|\), with reflection in the y-axis if \(c<0\). A negative outside multiplier reflects in the x-axis. Describe an ordered sequence or give an unambiguous coordinate rule.

Find the new domain by putting \(cx+d\) in the old domain. Find the new range by applying \(ay+b\) to the old range; reverse the endpoint order if \(a<0\).

Recall later

Under \(y=2f(x-1)+3\), the point \((4,-2)\) moves to \((5,-1)\).

examples.solution_html: The new coordinates are \((u-2,v-3)\): translate 2 units left and 3 units down. The inside plus sign moves the graph left.
Solve \(3x=6\), so the new input is 2. The new output is \(2(-1)=-2\). The image is \((2,-2)\): horizontal scale factor 1/3, vertical scale factor 2.

examples.question_html: Find the vertex and range of \(y=-(x+1)^2+4\).
examples.solution_html: Starting with \(x^2\), translate left 1, reflect in the x-axis, then translate up 4. The vertex is \((-1,4)\). The range is \(y\le4\).

common_mistakes: Using the inside scale factor instead of its reciprocal.
Translating vertically before stretching when the given formula requires the other order.
Forgetting to transform domain or range endpoints.

problems.title: Reversing a decreasing function on an interval
problems.objective: Transfer a closed interval through a decreasing mapping and solve a fixed-point equation.
problems.stem_html: The function \(f\) is defined by \(f(x)=5-3x\) for \(-1\le x\le4\).
problems.hint_html: Compare the two endpoint outputs. The inverse domain is the original range.

parts.solution_html: The function decreases: \(f(-1)=8\) and \(f(4)=-7\). Every intermediate value is attained, so the range is \(-7\le y\le8\).

criteria.requirement: Give the inclusive interval [−7,8] in the correct order.

parts.alternative_methods: A monotonicity argument with endpoint substitution is sufficient.
parts.common_error: Keeping the endpoint order of the inputs after a decreasing mapping.
parts.label: a

parts.solution_html: From \(y=5-3x\), \(x=(5-y)/3\). Exchange the names to obtain the inverse; its domain is the range from part (a).
parts.alternative_methods: A direct reversal of the arithmetic operations is accepted.
parts.common_error: Using [−1,4] as the inverse domain.
parts.label: b

parts.solution_html: On the common domain \([-1,4]\), solve \((5-x)/3=5-3x\). This gives \(8x=10\), hence \(x=5/4\), which is permitted. Both outputs are \(5/4\).

criteria.requirement: Check the value lies in both domains.

parts.alternative_methods: Solving f(x)=x is accepted here if the equivalence for this particular linear function is justified.
parts.common_error: Ignoring the domain check or assuming a general inverse-intersection rule.
parts.label: c

problems.title: A fractional inverse with a missing output
problems.objective: Find an excluded range value and reverse a fractional mapping.
problems.hint_html: Write the numerator as \(2(x-1)+5\). Keep every denominator restriction.

parts.prompt_html: Write \(f(x)\) as \(a+b/(x-1)\), and state its range.
parts.solution_html: Since \(2x+3=2(x-1)+5\), the required form follows. The fraction cannot be zero, so the output cannot be 2. Conversely every real y other than 2 gives a valid input \(x=1+5/(y-2)\).

criteria.requirement: Exclude exactly the output 2, with a nonzero-fraction justification.

parts.alternative_methods: Rearranging y=f(x) and showing all y≠2 are attainable is accepted.
parts.common_error: Excluding the input value 1 from the range instead of the output value 2.
parts.label: a

criteria.requirement: Collect original x-terms correctly after cross-multiplication.
State x≠2 as the inverse domain.

parts.alternative_methods: Equivalent algebraic forms are accepted.
parts.common_error: Cancelling terms across a sum or losing the excluded value.
parts.label: b

parts.solution_html: \(x+3=4(x-2)\), giving \(x=11/3\). This is not the excluded value 2. Equivalently, x=f(4)=11/3.

criteria.requirement: Use a correct equation or the inverse relation x=f(4).

parts.alternative_methods: Evaluating f(4) directly is accepted.
parts.common_error: Returning 4 as the input rather than reversing the mapping.
parts.label: c

problems.title: When two orders happen to agree
problems.objective: Distinguish composition orders, solve their equality and find a composite range.
problems.hint_html: Write both compositions before expanding. Equality for a few inputs does not make the two functions identical.

parts.alternative_methods: Unexpanded but correct expressions earn the relevant substitution criterion; simplification is required for its accuracy criterion.
parts.common_error: Reversing composition order or omitting the cross term in a square.
parts.label: a

parts.solution_html: Equating gives \(2x^2+3=4x^2-4x+3\), hence \(2x(x-2)=0\). Both roots 0 and 2 are allowed.

criteria.requirement: Reduce to a correct factored equation.

parts.alternative_methods: Any valid quadratic solution method is accepted.
parts.common_error: Dividing by x and losing zero.
parts.label: b

parts.solution_html: Since \(x^2\ge0\), the minimum of \(2x^2+3\) is 3 at x=0. Every greater value is attained, so the range is y≥3.
parts.alternative_methods: A graph or completed-square argument is accepted.
parts.common_error: Finding the range of gf instead of the requested composition.
parts.label: c

problems.title: Square roots in two different orders
problems.objective: Enforce the intermediate domain and check a squared equation.
problems.stem_html: Let \(f(x)=\sqrt{x+1}\), with domain \(x\ge-1\), and \(g(x)=3x-2\), with real domain.
problems.hint_html: For fg, the output of g must be at least −1. For gf, start from the domain of f.

parts.solution_html: \(f(g(x))=\sqrt{(3x-2)+1}=\sqrt{3x-1}\). Its radicand must be nonnegative, giving x≥1/3.
parts.alternative_methods: The equivalent requirement g(x)≥−1 is accepted.
parts.common_error: Using the domain x≥−1 for both orders.
parts.label: a

parts.solution_html: Apply f first: \(g(f(x))=3\sqrt{x+1}-2\). The linear outer function imposes no further restriction, so x≥−1.
parts.alternative_methods: A mapping-domain explanation is accepted.
parts.common_error: Putting the outer subtraction inside the square root.
parts.label: b

parts.solution_html: \(\sqrt{3x-1}=2\) implies \(3x-1=4\), so x=5/3. This lies in the domain and substitution gives the positive output 2.

criteria.requirement: Give x=5/3 and accept it after a domain/substitution check.

parts.alternative_methods: A correct inverse mapping calculation is accepted.
parts.common_error: Squaring without checking the original nonnegative square-root output.
parts.label: c

problems.title: Choosing the right-hand branch
problems.objective: Connect one-to-one behaviour, the inverse branch and its domain/range.
problems.hint_html: On this branch x−2 is nonnegative. That determines the square-root sign.

parts.prompt_html: Explain why \(f\) is one-to-one on its domain, and state its range.
parts.solution_html: As x increases from 2, the nonnegative quantity x−2 increases, so its square strictly increases. Thus no output is repeated. The minimum is −3 at x=2 and there is no upper bound.

criteria.requirement: Justify one-to-one behaviour on the stated right-hand branch.

parts.alternative_methods: A correct monotonic graph or derivative argument is accepted; a zero derivative at the endpoint does not prevent strict increase.
parts.common_error: Claiming that every quadratic is one-to-one.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find \(f^{-1}(x)\), its domain and its range.
parts.solution_html: From y=(x−2)²−3, take x−2=√(y+3) because x≥2. Hence the inverse is 2+√(x+3). Its domain is the original range and its range is the original domain.

criteria.requirement: Choose and obtain the positive-branch inverse 2+√(x+3).

parts.alternative_methods: Rearrangement with an explicit branch check is accepted.
parts.common_error: Giving ±√ as if the inverse could have two outputs.
parts.label: b

parts.solution_html: 2+√(x+3)=6 gives √(x+3)=4, so x=13. It is in the inverse domain. Equivalently x=f(6)=13.

criteria.requirement: Use a valid inverse equation or x=f(6).

parts.alternative_methods: Direct evaluation of f(6) is accepted.
parts.common_error: Squaring 6 before subtracting 2.
parts.label: c

problems.title: The largest left-branch endpoint
problems.objective: Find the maximal branch restriction and reject the root outside it.
problems.hint_html: Complete the square. If the domain extends beyond the vertex it contains a pair of equal-output inputs.

parts.prompt_html: Find the greatest value of \(a\) for which \(f\) is one-to-one, explaining why it is greatest.
parts.solution_html: \(f(x)=(x-3)^2+4\). It strictly decreases on x≤3, so a=3 works. For any a>3 choose a sufficiently small t>0 with 3+t≤a. Both 3−t and 3+t are in the domain and have equal outputs, so no larger a works.

criteria.requirement: Locate the vertex at x=3 and identify the one-to-one left branch.
State a=3 and explain why any larger endpoint repeats an output.

parts.alternative_methods: A precise graph argument using symmetric inputs is accepted.
parts.common_error: Giving a<3 as the greatest value or merely finding the vertex without considering larger a.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Using this greatest \(a\), find \(f^{-1}(x)\) and its domain.
parts.solution_html: On x≤3, solve y=(x−3)²+4 using x−3=−√(y−4). Thus the inverse is 3−√(x−4), with domain x≥4.
parts.alternative_methods: An equivalent rearranged formula is accepted.
parts.common_error: Selecting the positive branch despite x≤3.
parts.label: b

parts.solution_html: (x−3)²=4 gives x=1 or 5. The domain x≤3 excludes 5, so the only solution is 1.

criteria.requirement: Reject 5 using the domain and give 1 only.

parts.alternative_methods: Evaluating f⁻¹(8)=1 with its branch justified is accepted.
parts.common_error: Keeping the root on the other branch.
parts.label: c

problems.title: A cubic and its reflected graph
problems.objective: Reflect points and find every common point of an increasing function and its inverse.
problems.hint_html: Swap coordinates when reflecting. For common points, use both equations; cubing is reversible for real numbers.

parts.solution_html: Cubing is strictly increasing on the real line. Reverse y=x³ to obtain x=∛y, so f⁻¹(x)=∛x for every real input.
parts.alternative_methods: An equivalent real-cube-root notation is accepted.
parts.common_error: Using a square root or excluding negative inputs.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: The point \(A=(2,8)\) is on the graph of \(f\). Give its reflection on the inverse graph and the line of reflection.
parts.solution_html: Reflection in y=x exchanges the coordinates, giving B=(8,2).
parts.alternative_methods: A labelled coordinate reflection is accepted.
parts.common_error: Changing signs instead of exchanging the coordinates.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find all common points of the two graphs.
parts.solution_html: Equate x³=∛x and cube both sides: x⁹=x. Thus x=0 or x⁸=1; for real x the latter gives x=±1. Substitution gives the three listed points, and all satisfy both original equations.

criteria.requirement: Use a complete method, such as the reversible equation x⁹=x.
Give all three matching coordinates and check the original equations.

parts.alternative_methods: Using strict increase to justify common points on y=x, then solving x³=x, is accepted.
parts.common_error: Assuming a common point must be on y=x without a valid argument or losing zero by division.
parts.label: c

problems.title: Reflected branches that never meet
problems.objective: Transfer graph features and justify the absence of intersections.
problems.hint_html: The function is strictly increasing on its branch. At a common point (u,v), both f(u)=v and f(v)=u must hold.

parts.prompt_html: Find the inverse and its domain.
parts.solution_html: Since the original x−1 is nonnegative, x−1=√(y−2). Exchanging variables gives 1+√(x−2), defined for x≥2.
parts.alternative_methods: A valid rearrangement with the branch condition is accepted.
parts.common_error: Using the negative branch or the original domain as the inverse domain.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: State the endpoint of the inverse graph, and the reflection of the point \((4,11)\).
parts.solution_html: The original branch starts at its vertex (1,2), so the inverse starts at (2,1). The point (4,11) reflects to (11,4).
parts.alternative_methods: Coordinate swapping with a clearly labelled endpoint is accepted.
parts.common_error: Leaving the endpoint coordinates unchanged.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Show that the graphs of \(f\) and \(f^{-1}\) have no common point.
parts.solution_html: If (u,v) is common, f(u)=v and f(v)=u. Strict increase rules out u<v and u>v, so u=v. A common point would therefore satisfy (u−1)²+2=u, or u²−3u+3=0. Its discriminant is 9−12=−3, so it has no real root and the graphs do not meet.

criteria.requirement: Justify why a common point must have equal coordinates for this increasing branch.
Obtain the fixed-point equation u²−3u+3=0 and its negative discriminant.
Conclude that there is no common point.

parts.alternative_methods: Showing f(x)>x for every permitted x also works: if f(u)=v then v>u, while f(v)=u would imply u>v, a contradiction.
parts.common_error: Using the fixed-point test for every inverse pair without justification.
parts.label: c

problems.title: Transforming a parabola in a specified order
problems.objective: Describe an ordered transformation and interpret its vertex, range and level set.
problems.hint_html: Inside changes affect x first; outside changes affect the output. Keep the final upward translation after the stretch and reflection.

parts.prompt_html: Describe a sequence of transformations taking \(y=f(x)\) to \(y=h(x)\).
parts.answer_html: Translate right 3; stretch vertically by factor 2 and reflect in the x-axis; then translate up 5.
parts.solution_html: First replace x by x−3, moving the graph right 3. Multiply outputs by −2: a vertical stretch of factor 2 and reflection in the x-axis, in either order. Finally add 5 to move it up 5.

criteria.requirement: Apply a vertical stretch of factor 2 and an x-axis reflection.
Translate up 5 after the output multiplication; the full sequence must produce the stated function.

parts.alternative_methods: Any other explicitly ordered sequence producing exactly −2f(x−3)+5 is accepted, as is the coordinate rule (u,v)→(u+3,−2v+5) with a correct description.
parts.common_error: Reflecting in the y-axis or stretching an already-translated vertical output without adjusting the translation.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: State the vertex and range of \(h\).
parts.solution_html: \(h(x)=-2(x-3)^2+5\), so its maximum is 5 at x=3. The downward branch has no lower bound.
parts.alternative_methods: Transforming the vertex (0,0) and the original range is accepted.
parts.common_error: Giving a minimum or the range y≥5.
parts.label: b

criteria.requirement: Rearrange to (x−3)²≤4 with the correct inequality sign.
Give the inclusive interval between them.

parts.alternative_methods: A graph/level intersection or expanded quadratic inequality is accepted.
parts.common_error: Failing to reverse the inequality on division by −2.
parts.label: c

problems.title: A transformed graph without an explicit formula
problems.objective: Use a coordinate mapping to transform a finite domain and range.
problems.stem_html: A function \(f\) has domain \([-2,4]\), range \([-1,7]\), and a point \((3,5)\) on its graph. Define \(h(x)=3f(2x+1)-4\).
problems.hint_html: Put 2x+1 in the original domain. Apply the outside transformation to the old output interval.

parts.solution_html: Require −2≤2x+1≤4. Subtract 1 and divide by 2 to obtain −3/2≤x≤3/2.
parts.alternative_methods: Mapping the two original domain endpoints using x=(u−1)/2 is accepted.
parts.common_error: Applying the outside factor 3 to the input interval.
parts.label: a

parts.solution_html: As 2x+1 covers the whole original domain, f attains every output in [−1,7]. The increasing output map v→3v−4 gives endpoints −7 and 17, so the range is [−7,17].

criteria.requirement: Apply the output map 3v−4 to the old range endpoints.

parts.alternative_methods: Interval arithmetic with an explanation that the whole original domain is covered is accepted.
parts.common_error: Transforming the range using the inside expression 2x+1.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Give the coordinate rule taking a point \((u,v)\) of \(f\) to its image on \(h\). Hence find the image of \((3,5)\).
parts.solution_html: The old input u equals 2x+1, so the new x-coordinate is (u−1)/2. The output becomes 3v−4. Thus (3,5) maps to ((3−1)/2,3·5−4)=(1,11).

criteria.requirement: Obtain the correctly paired image point (1,11).

parts.alternative_methods: A horizontal scale factor 1/2 followed by translation left 1/2, then output stretch 3 and translation down 4, is accepted if the requested coordinate rule is clear.
parts.common_error: Using 2u+1 as the new x-coordinate.
parts.label: c
